lessonSettings.about: Everything specific to one Atlas app and its Hub lives in <name>-lessons.json next to this file and is merged over these shared settings. The default is built into resources/dist, which the publishing notebook reads; every other one is built into resources/dist/<name>. Pages use the default unless the address has ?lessons=<name>; the build and the checker take --lessons <name> (or --all).

aiPrompt.about: Prompt teachers can paste into the AI tool their school allows. The lesson's map, layers, bookmarks and questions are added after these rules, from the lesson file, so the prompt never names a layer the map doesn't have.
aiPrompt.label: Prompt for your own AI
rules: You are helping a teacher make classroom questions for a {lessonKind} lesson. The map, its layers, what each pop-up shows, its bookmarks and the questions already written are listed below.

Use only the layers, pop-up contents and bookmarks listed. Do not invent layers, tools, data or map features. If a question would need information this map does not show, say so instead of inventing it.

Every question must be answerable by a student who opens the map{inApp} and uses it: clicking pop-ups, reading the legend, using bookmarks, measuring or turning layers on and off. Name the exact layer or bookmark a student should use.
Write for grade 8 (age 13 to 14), in short sentences. Do not include answers unless the teacher asks for them, and never write material for students that contains the answers.

{theApp} has these tools: Basemaps, Open map, Map layers (turn layers on and off), Add layer, Legend, Measure ({measureUnits}), Sketch, 2D/3D, Bookmarks and pop-ups. It has no time slider or filter unless listed below. A pop-up that says 1 of 2 means more than one feature is at that spot; use the arrows to see each one.

teaching.about: Standing teacher-guide text shared by every lesson. A lesson can give its own instructionalModels list. The last line of What every lesson includes comes from assistant.howItWorks in the lessons settings file, or promptOnly when there is no assistant.
prep: Open the map and click through the bookmarks and pop-ups. Check the legend at the zoom levels the questions use; it changes as you zoom and as layers are turned on and off.
Decide whether students work alone, in pairs or as a whole class, and whether they use the printed sheet or a digital copy.
Encourage students to look for patterns and make observations, not just to find the right answers.
Layers the questions don't use are there for further study.
teaching.materials: The lesson includes the {appMap}, a two-page Word student sheet in English and Spanish, and these teacher notes. Print the sheet, or download it and upload it to Google Drive to edit it in Google Docs (it also opens in Word). The Google Classroom button shares the map, not the sheet; to assign the sheet, attach your Drive copy in Classroom with Make a copy for each student, or paste the map link and attach the sheet yourself. No account or login is needed. Sketches on the map are not saved between sessions.
howTheyWork: Each lesson is one {appMap} and a set of questions that students answer by using the map: opening bookmarks, clicking pop-ups, reading the legend, turning layers on and off and measuring. The questions can't be answered from a textbook alone.
Students need no account or login. {openInApp} opens the map straight from the lesson page; the Share to Google Classroom button shares the map link with a class.

The Word student sheet (English and Spanish) is two pages: a big question, some background, help reading the map, the questions with space to write, and a closing reflection. Print it or share it digitally; it opens in Word and Google Docs.
Each lesson page lists the questions with the exact steps for the front of the class, marks one question as the one to use if you only have 15 minutes, and gives ideas for support and stretch.
Where to find each answer on the map, and what to accept, are on a separate answer page and in the Word teacher notes, so the lesson page can be shared with students.
Sketches on the map are not saved between sessions. Students who sketch should finish in one session or take a screenshot.
teaching.promptOnly: Each lesson page has a prompt to paste into an AI tool, which lists the map's layers so the tool doesn't invent any.

rubric.about: Shared rubric for the answer to each lesson's compelling question. Four criteria, four levels; a lesson adds its own line about what counts as map evidence (lesson assessment.evidence). Shown on How these lessons work, each answer page and the Word teacher notes. Teachers can use it as it is, adapt it or ignore it.

criteria.name: Claim
descriptors: No clear answer to the big question, or restates the question.
Gives an answer, but it is vague or only partly about the big question.
Gives a clear answer to the big question.
Gives a clear answer and says how far it holds (for example, where or when it does not).

criteria.name: Map evidence
descriptors: No evidence from the map, or evidence that is not on the map.
One piece of evidence from the map, or evidence that is not specific (no names, dates or numbers).
Specific evidence from at least two layers or places on the map: named features, dates, numbers or distances read from pop-ups, the legend or Measure.
Specific evidence from at least two layers or places, chosen to fit the claim, with the layer or feature named so a reader could find it.

criteria.name: Geographic reasoning
descriptors: Lists facts without connecting them to the answer.
Connects some evidence to the answer, but the link is not explained.
Explains how the evidence supports the answer, including where things happened and why there.
Explains where and why, and notes a pattern, a change over time or a connection between layers.

criteria.name: Accuracy
descriptors: Several facts do not match the map.
Mostly matches the map, with one or two mistakes.
Dates, places, winners, numbers and distances match the map.
Everything matches the map, and the answer says where on the map it came from.
